voyage.name: Fire Museum
voyage.content: Three fire-fighting helicopters, ten trucks, and 3 floors of exhibitions. Very popular with kids, who can wear fire-fighting clothes and ride some of the helicopters and trucks.

voyage.name: Hanazono Shrine
voyage.address: near the intersection of Meiji-dori and Yasukuni-dori
voyage.content: More remarkable for its location than its appearance, but it's a nice place to take a breather. There's often a flea market in the surrounding park on weekends.

voyage.name: Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden
voyage.hours: 09:00-16:30; open until 18:00 mid-March to June and mid-August to September, until 19:00 July to mid-August. Closed Mondays (with some exceptions) and during the New Year's Holiday
voyage.content: A large public garden, and one of the most popular places for viewing cherry blossoms in spring. It has Japanese, English and French gardens, as well as a Taiwanese teahouse and a greenhouse. The entrance fee often makes the park surprisingly uncrowded and peaceful. Admission ends 30 minutes before closing.

voyage.name: Shinjuku-sanchōme and related red-light districts to the east of the station
voyage.content: It is perfectly safe to walk around here during the day and marvel at the photo billboards of various male and female escorts on offer as well as the live gangster-types acting shady. While it probably shouldn't be done with children, for adults the result is far more "cultural interest" than sleaze.

voyage.name: Shinjuku Southern Terrace
voyage.alt: ja 新宿サザンテラス
voyage.address: across from the South Exit of Shinjuku Station
voyage.content: The promenade next to the Southern Terrace exit offers a magnificent view of the Takashimaya department store and a bridge that offers the best spot for watching trains enter and exit. Starbucks, Shake Shack and other restaurants.

voyage.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Center
voyage.content: The two enormous buildings of this giant hive of bureaucracy are an Orwellian architectural masterpiece designed by noted architect Kenzo Tange. The main reasons to come here, though, are the twin observatories. At a height of 202 m on the 45th floor, they have some of the best views of Tokyo. The North Observatory is open daily from 09:30 to 23:00 (closed second and fourth Mondays of each month), while the South Obs

voyage.name: Tokyo Opera City
voyage.alt: ja 東京オペラシティ
voyage.content: A building complex with a skyscraper. Housing the New National Theatre Tokyo, concert halls, two art museums (one specialized in multimedia art), many shops and restaurants.

voyage.name: Tokyo Toy Museum
voyage.alt: ja 東京おもちゃ美術館 Tokyo omocha bijutsukan
voyage.content: An old school filled with toys and fun small houses. Accompanying adults won't get bored, thanks to the variety of toys.

voyage.name: Suga Shrine
voyage.alt: ja 東京四谷総鎮守 須賀神社
voyage.content: It is a shrine located around Shinjuku. It is a small shrine, but the stairs in front of it are famous as the background in the animated movie Your Name.

voyage.name: Japan National Stadium
voyage.content: Completed in 2019 as the main stadium for the Summer Games Tokyo 2020.

voyage.name: Meiji Jingu Stadium
voyage.content: Known as Jingu Stadium. Can see university and professional baseball games. It is also famous for being a stadium for the Tokyo qualifying round of the National High School Baseball Tournament.

voyage.name: Karaokekan
voyage.content: Karaokekan is a large chain of karaoke shops. They have rooms available from one person up to a large party. All you can drink set menus are available.

voyage.name: Club on the Park Spa
voyage.address: Park Hyatt Tokyo Hotel, 3-7-1-2 Nishi Shinjuku

voyage.name: Shinjuku Piccadilly
voyage.content: The newest movie theater in Shinjuku. It features stadium seating and "platinum" seating. Platinum seating ranges from a semi-private room, including a private lounge (¥5000 per person) to a private room, including a relaxation room (¥30,000 for 2 people).

voyage.name: Wald 9
voyage.content: Part of the new generation of movie theaters in Tokyo. It features stadium seating, a small gift shop, and clean theaters.

voyage.name: Cinem@rt Shinjuku
voyage.content: 335 seats total. Mondays are Men's Days, when men can watch movies for ¥1000. Wednesdays are Ladies' Days, when ladies can watch movies for only ¥1000.

voyage.name: Isetan
voyage.content: Isetan is the most prestigious department store in Shinjuku and boasts the highest sales figures in Japan. It caters to a broad adult age group. It has a beautiful depachika (basement floor selling food and gifts) that is a little more expensive than other department stores in Shinjuku.

voyage.name: Keio
voyage.content: Keio is similar to the Odakyu department store in terms of goods and services. The depachika is smaller and more cramped than other department stores.

voyage.name: Lumine
voyage.content: Lumine has 3 buildings around the JR Shinjuku Station. Lumine 1 and 2 cater to all ages with average priced goods. Both buildings are at the South Exit. Lumine Est (ja ルミネエスト) is at the East Exit and Central East Exit. Lumine Est focuses more on haute fashion for younger women and famous restaurants.

voyage.name: Marui
voyage.content: Marui is well known department store known for focusing on the 16-32 year age group. Spread out around Shinjuku Sanchome, the main building is next to Shinjuku Gyoen. The men's building is north of the main building and Marui Young is west of Isetan.

voyage.name: Mylord
voyage.content: Cloths department store run by Odakyu, targeted at younger age group.

voyage.name: Odakyu
voyage.content: Odakyu was closed in 2022 for re-development of the area and moved to the smaller Halc building, north of the West Bus Loop, which also houses the electronics store Bic Camera.

voyage.name: Takashimaya
voyage.alt: ja タカシマヤ新宿店
voyage.content: This department store caters towards the mid-20s and up, along with families. The depachika is comparable to Isetan, but not as famous. Look for Hands and Books Kinokuniya at the Southern end of the department store.

voyage.name: Hands
voyage.content: This is a large variety goods shop, and if "large" doesn't impress you, you have probably never faced the dilemma which kind of sand to use for your model railway. Because here, you can choose from a dozen kinds of sand alone - from yellow Sahara sand to reddish Nullarbor sand, everything in handy plastic packets. This shop is the best proof that in a rich mega city, there is a clientele for anything. You can buy alm

voyage.name: Bookoff
voyage.content: Bookoff is a well-known second-hand book store. They also offer various albums, games, and movies.

voyage.name: Books Kinokuniya
voyage.content: Books Kinokuniya is the best book store for foreign language books. The Main Branch is the older of the two, however, the Southern Branch has a greater selection of foreign language books.

voyage.name: Book 1st
voyage.content: The largest bookstore on the west side is hidden underground. Navigation inside may be a pain for its unusual layout. English books are in the C3 area.

voyage.name: Bic Camera
voyage.content: Second-largest electronics shop in Shinjuku. While not as big as Yodobashi Camera, prices and product range is roughly the same. The East side shop, next to Books Kinokuniya, is bigger than Yodobashi's East side shop, but still smaller than the West side location.

voyage.name: Yodobashi Camera
voyage.content: Yodobashi is the largest electronics retailer in Shinjuku. The main building is their multimedia centre. They also have a dedicated building each for Games, Camera, Travel, Watch and Mobile/smartphone (with a liquor section in the basement). Yodobashi also has a branch on the east side of Shinjuku, across from Lumine EST.

voyage.name: Don Quijote Kabukicho store
voyage.alt: ja ドン・キホーテ don kihōte
voyage.content: A hectic 24-hour discount store that sells just about everything that you would never imagine needing at 03:00 but might just pick up anyway, such as clothing, bicycles, electronics, jewelry, and gag gifts.

voyage.name: Don Quijote Southeast Exit store
voyage.content: Newer branch near the station.

voyage.name: Disk Union
voyage.content: You can get music, movies, and music books. Another branch at Shinjuku 3-17-5 specialize in specific genres or used goods. Great for music enthusiasts.

voyage.name: HMV
voyage.content: HMV is one of the bigger record stores in Japan with a good selection of music and movies. Another store at Shinjuku Alta 6F.

voyage.name: Tower Records
voyage.content: Tower Records is one of the biggest record stores in Japan. They have any CD or DVD you can imagine, and if not, you can probably order or reserve it.

voyage.name: Nishi-Shinjuku 7-chome
voyage.content: Packed with music shops specializing in various genres such as punk and heavy metal. Many sell nothing but bootlegs and collectibles.

voyage.name: West Exit Square Event Space
voyage.alt: ja 西口広場イベントスペース
voyage.content: An area hosting a rotating series of stalls or exhibits. These have included various local foods from around Japan, furniture, art prints and information about various government projects around Tokyo. The underground area around it is a great place to find takeaway food and fast food outlets - named Keio Mall, Odakyu Ace and Shinjuku Delish Park (temporary location for Odakyu's depachika).

voyage.name: Pasutakan
voyage.content: Okonomiyaki cooked at your table.

voyage.name: Khao San
voyage.content: A good place for Thai street-stall style food. It's always packed and hectic for lunch, with attendants hollering to attract customers.

voyage.name: Blumare
voyage.content: Pizza and pasta restaurant. The building is full of restaurants all run by Sapporo Beer.

voyage.name: Suzuya
voyage.content: This tonkatsu restaurant is famous for its green tea tonkatsu, which is salty and filling. It also serves other types of tonkatsu and katsudon.

voyage.name: Martiniburger
voyage.alt: ja マティーニバーガー
voyage.content: This restaurant serves hamburgers and martinis. The large juicy hamburgers are made with high quality ground beef, which is very hard to find anywhere in Japan. Though uncommon, the combination of hamburgers and martinis is surprisingly nice.

voyage.name: Acacia Shinjuku
voyage.alt: ja アカシア新宿本店
voyage.content: Specialises in cabbage rolls. Also has a set menu with hashed rice and pork sauté. Has a branch at Haneda Airport.

voyage.name: Botejyu
voyage.content: Botejyu is an okonomiyaki shop that sells a variety of okonomiyaki. They also have various yaki-soba dishes. Beware that at times, this restaurant can be busy with wait times of up to 30 min.

voyage.name: Juttoku
voyage.content: This izakaya has an excellent selection of sake.

voyage.name: Kappō Nakajima
voyage.content: Specializes in sardine dishes. Yanagawa teishoku is deep-fried sardines with scrambled eggs on rice (it tastes better than it sounds).

voyage.name: Hokkaido
voyage.address: 53rd floor of Tokyo Opera City (see above)
voyage.content: Enjoy the view while dining on seafood and other specialties of Hokkaido. Got another branch near Shinjuku station (9F 110 Building).

voyage.name: Yanbaru
voyage.content: Now occupying the whole of a three-story building, there's nothing pretentious about this restaurant specializing in Okinawan food, which emphasizes pork and vegetables that are unusual even to Honshu Japanese. Recommend is beni imo korokke (¥480), tempura-style sweet potato; and hechima misoni (¥620), an eggplant-like vegetable served in a strongly fermented miso sauce. A picture menu is available.

voyage.name: Bosphorus Hasan
voyage.alt: ja ボスボラスハサン
voyage.content: Authentic Turkish food. HALAL food.

voyage.name: Din Tai Fung
voyage.content: Tokyo branch of the renowned Taiwan dim sum restaurant; speciality is the xiǎolóngbāo (zh-Hant 小籠包) soup-in dumplings.

voyage.name: Nabezo
voyage.content: An all-you-can-eat Shabu Shabu restaurant with another branch in Shinjuku and many other places. \3850 gets one person 100 minutes, including unlimited meat, veggies, and ice cream. Drinks cost extra, but water and Gobo cha are free. If 100 minutes isn't enough, extend 30 minutes for additional \550.

voyage.name: Onegiya Shinjuku ten
voyage.content: Excellent traditional but modern Japanese restaurant. Plenty of dishes to order but you need to like leeks.

voyage.name: Zauo
voyage.content: Indoor fishing and restaurant combined at dinner time...(click the link and see photos). No fishing on weekday lunch time.

voyage.name: Torafugu-Tei
voyage.content: Specializing in the infamous fugu (blowfish), it's one of the huge number of seafood restaurants in Kabukichō (see below). Set dinners go for around ¥5000, featuring fugu prepared five or six ways, fresh from the tank. Has another branch nearby (at 1-3-15 Kabukicho).

voyage.name: Araku
voyage.content: Australian-run, considerably larger and can be less intimidating than many other Golden Gai establishments.

voyage.name: Bar K
voyage.content: Always welcoming of foreigners with beers.

voyage.name: Hair of The Dogs
voyage.content: Punk rock with a dash of Mexican Luchadors. Good cocktails and beer at an average of ¥700 a drink. The owner, Tohru, is very welcoming to anyone who loves to rock. Cover charge lets you sit at the bar and choose music from a menu split into various Punk Rock styles (UK, USA, Japan, Hardcore, Goth, Oi, Mod, Post Punk, 70s, 80s etc). Movies like Taxi Driver and Sid & Nancy are played from a cheap projector to the wall

voyage.name: Bar Albatross-G
voyage.content: Casual cocktail bar with Burgundy painted walls, chandeliers and no-frills mixology. Cover charge includes a small snack of either noodles, miso or whatever's brewing. Most drinks are around ¥700. Space includes a second floor "attic" accessible by a thin staircase with more fixtures and local artists' creations. Also visit the original Albatross bar in Shinjuku Omoide-Yokocho.

voyage.name: Rock Bar: Mother
voyage.content: Has an extensive collection of Punk and Metal CDs for those looking for some alternative rock.

voyage.name: Godz Bar
voyage.content: Heavy metal/hard rock bar.

voyage.name: Champion
voyage.address: Just before the Golden Gai entrance and slightly west as you head back towards Kabukichō
voyage.content: Staffed mostly by Filipinas who speak excellent English.

voyage.name: New York Bar & Grill
voyage.content: One of the main sets for Lost in Translation, this slick joint on the 52nd floor has dark decor and floor-to-ceiling windows with jaw-dropping vistas, with live jazz nightly. Eating a steak here would cost you well north of ¥20,000 per head, but you can nurse a beer for a mere ¥1000 or, "for relaxing times", try out Bill Murray's Suntory Hibiki for ¥3,500.

voyage.name: Casablanca
voyage.content: A two level nightclub and lounge with a large dance floor and darts. The DJ normally spins hip-hop, R&B, reggae, and house, and there are live house performances periodically through the night.

voyage.name: Loft/Plus One
voyage.alt: ja ロフトプラスワン
voyage.content: Performance art space meets bar run with a simple concept: different people and groups rent a block of time and do whatever they want to. The end result runs from stand-up comedy and lectures to porn star photo shoots and incredibly violent live S&M. Erotic shows 18+ only (ID required).

voyage.name: Tokyo Loose
voyage.content: Small bar full of men. It's not easy to find, so call for directions.

voyage.name: Adezakura
voyage.content: Lesbian bar.

voyage.name: AiiRO Cafe
voyage.content: Cruisy open-air bar with a torii gate at the entrance. Crowd spilling onto the street makes it feel like a block party.

voyage.name: Arty Farty
voyage.content: Among Nichō's most well-known pubs, with a thumping dance floor. A hand stamp upon entry will also get you into sister bar The Annex.

voyage.name: Campy! Bar
voyage.content: "Mix bar". Has another branch at Shibuya PARCO.

voyage.name: Dragon Men
voyage.content: Masculine gay pub with a dance floor. Rebuilt after a fire, the place is popular among male and female foreigners, and with Japanese men.

voyage.name: GB
voyage.content: Relaxed basement bar with somewhat more mature crowds.

voyage.name: Gold Finger
voyage.content: Primarily lesbian bar with all-female staff, and karaoke for the multinational patrons. Interior themed like a 1970s motel. Saturday is strictly women-only; Monday is FtM night.

voyage.name: New Sazae
voyage.content: Bar with dancefloor known for attracting bisexual crowds.

voyage.name: Vox
voyage.content: Another mix bar.

voyage.name: Akha Ama
voyage.content: Specialty coffee from northern Thailand.

voyage.name: Doutor
voyage.content: Doutor is a relatively "salary man" coffee shop. You will see lots of business men within this shop. Non-smoking, with some shops equipped with smoking booths.

voyage.name: Excelsior Caffe
voyage.content: Excelsior Caffe and Doutor are run by the same company, however Excelsior Caffe caters to a younger, more feminine crowd and one-notch upscale. Generally non-smoking, with bigger shops have separate smoking rooms.

voyage.name: Pronto/Di Punto
voyage.hours: Cafe style opens in the morning and closes around 17:30. Then bar opens within minutes
voyage.content: Pronto is a very relaxed cafe/bar that is a cafe during the day. They offer premium style drinks.

voyage.name: Segafredo Zanetti Espresso
voyage.address: 3 locations near Shinjuku Station and another in Tokyo Opera City
voyage.content: Segafredo is a somewhat upscale Italian style cafe that has various locations near Shinjuku. Segafredo tends to have a darker atmosphere akin to Pronto and offers many kinds of alcoholic drinks too.

voyage.name: Canal Cafe
voyage.content: In the far east of Shinjuku City in the Kagurazaka district. With views remarkable for Tokyo, Canal Cafe consists of a separate restaurant and cafe situated alongside a canal. The open-air cafe has great ambiance. At the restaurant figure ¥6000-9000 for dinner, but at the café, which is a long patio-like dock, drinks and snacks are purchased at the bar and can be quite reasonable.

voyage.name: Tajimaya Coffee house
voyage.content: Truely classic kissaten (full-service coffee shop).

voyage.name: Tokiya
voyage.content: Japanese sweets and drinks. Famous for dorayaki, drum-shaped cake with red-bean paste inside.

voyage.name: HUB
voyage.content: Popular chain of cash-on-delivery English pubs. Have some fish and chips with your pint at one of four Shinjuku locations. "82 Ale House" pubs are run by the same company with wider selection of whiskeys.

voyage.name: Marone
voyage.content: Tucked away in this tiny cubbyhole of a space is one of the most interesting small bars in Tokyo. A country western theme with Chet Baker and Nat King Cole pouring from the stereo. The food is cheap and superbly done (think chili nachos and the like); beer and spirits are also available. The place is tiny but it attracts a great mix of young groups of friends and office workers. Some nights Marone puts on live music

voyage.name: Vagabond
voyage.content: A great little pub with two floors. The first floor is a little more private while the top floor is a very cozy jazz bar with live music and a good selection of finger foods cooked right at the bar for you. Caution to taller travelers: it's a little cramped at the bar. Cover charge and drinks are ¥500-700. The pub usually closes around 23:00 to 23:30 leaving you with plenty of time to get the last train.

voyage.name: Sakura Hotel Hatagaya
voyage.alt: ja サクラホテル幡ヶ谷
voyage.price: Single rooms ¥6930, double rooms ¥9000, twin & triple room with breakfast
voyage.content: Affordable hotel with a round-the-clock cafe offering a variety of Asian ethnic dishes. Staff can speak English.

voyage.name: Tama Ryokan
voyage.price: Prices for one person no higher than ¥4,500, and the prices drop if more than 1 person stays per room
voyage.content: There is a lounge for relaxing and internet access.

voyage.name: Manboo Internet & Comic Cafe
voyage.content: Internet cafe that has small, private rooms to crash out in. Rooms have a comfortable reclining chair (or a "flat seat" option), internet, TV, and headphones. Free soft drinks and coffee are provided and there's also a shower room/toilet and toiletries on sale. Three locations near the station.

voyage.name: Ace Inn Shinjuku
voyage.price: Rooms from ¥3150, long term discount starting from 1 week
voyage.content: Capsule Hotel. On the ninth floor there is a common space with vending machines and TV, where you can meet with the other guests from all over the world. Internet connection via WiFi in the whole building or PC on the ground level is free. English speaking staff.

voyage.name: Hotel Sunroute Plaza Shinjuku
voyage.alt: ja ホテルサンルートプラザ新宿
voyage.content: Includes a restaurant, a bar, and massage parlor. Recommended for taller guests. (Better rates are often available by the usual Western online booking agents.).

voyage.name: Shinjuku Prince Hotel
voyage.alt: ja 新宿プリンスホテル
voyage.content: Includes restaurants, a bakery, and salon.

voyage.name: Hotel Sunlite Shinjuku
voyage.alt: ja ホテルサンライト新宿
voyage.price: Singles start at ¥8,715; doubles at ¥12,075 per night. Discounts are offered if you refer to their web page

voyage.name: Tokyu Stay Yotsuya
voyage.price: Singles start at ¥9,450; doubles at ¥17,850 per night. Slight discounts are offered for extended stays
voyage.content: Part of the Tokyu Stay chain, these hotels are popular with business travelers. The small kitchenettes, washer/dryers, and free LAN access in all rooms makes these a good value.

voyage.name: Hyatt Regency Tokyo
voyage.alt: ja ハイアットリージェンシー東京
voyage.content: 744 rooms and suites with views of Mt Fuji and Shinjuku Central Park. Regency Club lounge for free continental breakfast, tea service and evening cocktails. Hosts a roof-top pool and healh spa.

voyage.name: Keio Plaza Hotel
voyage.alt: ja 京王プラザホテル
voyage.content: You can see the city view of Tokyo, and the rooms are spacious. Free Wi-Fi and bicycle sharing services exist.

voyage.name: Hotel Century Southern Tower
voyage.alt: ja 小田急ホテルセンチュリーサザンタワー
voyage.content: Well furnished rooms with enough space to get around it. Very good breakfast buffet. Excellent views of the surrounding area from rooms and lobby, which is on the 20th floor.

voyage.name: Park Hyatt Tokyo
voyage.alt: ja パークハイアット東京
voyage.content: Towering above the rest literally and figuratively, this hotel is best known for featuring prominently in the movie Lost in Translation. Surprisingly intimate in feel, one of the standout features is the 47th-floor "Club on the Park" pool with floor-to-ceiling views of Shinjuku at night. The New York Bar on the 51st floor also offers superior views at night. Service and amenities are superlative, but rates are astron

voyage.name: Hilton Tokyo
voyage.content: It has rooms that face the Shinjuku Metropolitan Government office. Has a nice underground shopping arcade named Hiltopia, which includes a Tourist Information center, a foreign bookstore, some restaurants and others.

voyage.name: Kimpton Shinjuku Tokyo
voyage.alt: ja キンプトン新宿東京
voyage.content: Luxury hotel featuring casual modern interior. Opened in 2020.

voyage.name: Sakura House
voyage.content: If you plan on staying in Tokyo for a month or more you might want to check this place out.

voyage.name: Tokyo International Forum
voyage.alt: 東京国際フォーラム, Tōkyō Kokusai Fōramu
voyage.address: located in front of Yurakuchō station
voyage.content: A massive, modern exhibition centre used for concerts, conventions and the like. On weekdays there are usually several food wagons selling boxed lunches, but aside from this there may not be much of interest to the casual tourist — except, of course, the impressive design. The atrium may be the most well-known symbol of the building, and one is able to stroll up the long, spiral walkway that runs along its glass-and-

voyage.name: mAAch ecute Kanda Manseibashi
voyage.alt: マーチエキュート神田万世橋
voyage.content: A historic train station that's been converted into a shopping mall. Besides interesting shops and cafes, there's also a library and history exhibits about the station, including a large diorama showing the area around the station as it was in 1912 when it opened.

voyage.name: National Diet Building
voyage.content: Housing Japan's bicameral legislature, it was built in the 1920s. The most recognizable symbol of the Japanese government, it was built from Japanese building materials, features a pyramidal roof and is surrounded with green areas. The nearby free Kensei Kinenkan (between the Diet and the water) has a nice view on it, and tons of political artefacts to satisfy those interested in Japanese politics. English tours are

voyage.name: Imperial Palace
voyage.content: Surrounded by a series of moats and high walls, the site of the former Edo Castle has been the official residence of the Japanese imperial family since 1868. Reputedly the most expensive square kilometre in the world, which during the height of Japan's bubble was estimated to be worth slightly more than California. The inner palace gardens and buildings are closed to the general public except on the second day of the

voyage.name: Imperial Palace East Garden
voyage.hours: Open daily except Mondays and Fridays
voyage.content: Kept in impeccable shape, the gardens of the Imperial Palace are particularly beautiful during the March and April plum and cherry blossom seasons. During the Edo period, this was the heart of the Shogun's castle, and you can see the tenshudai, the raised platform where the tenshukaku (main keep) was once located, and an open field that was once the site of the honmaru goten, the Shogun's main residential palace. Ent

voyage.name: Kitanomaru Park
voyage.content: Connected to the East Gardens on the north side is this park. Offering much of the same, it is a convenient way to get to Yasukuni Shrine. The park also houses the Nippon Budōkan (日本武道館), which regularly stages martial arts competitions and live concerts, as well as the Kagaku Gijyutsukan (科学技術館, Science museum).

voyage.name: Chidoriga-fuchi Moat
voyage.address: on the northwest side of the Imperial gardens grounds
voyage.content: One of, if not the most prominent cherry blossom site in Tokyo, and attracts throngs of people in its March-to-April peak season. It is located just across the street from Yasukuni-shrine. Rowboats are also available for one to row along a limited portion of the moat at ¥500 for 30 minutes, ¥1000 for an hour and at a slightly more expensive rate during cherry blossom periods.

voyage.name: Yūshūkan War Memorial Museum
voyage.price: Adult ¥1000, post-secondary student ¥500, high school student ¥300, child free
voyage.content: An odd collection of military paraphernalia (including human torpedoes and letters from kamikaze pilots) and one-sided (allegedly revisionist according to the Chinese, Koreans and other Asian countries except Taiwan) descriptions of Imperial Japan and World War II, but it can be pretty confronting at times. The museum includes a small military history book and model shop.

voyage.name: Holy Resurrection Cathedral
voyage.content: A beautifully-restored 1800s-vintage Russian Orthodox cathedral located near Ochanomizu Station on the Chuo Line. Use the Hijiribashi exit. The Hijiribashi bridge by the exit is one of the better looking bridges in Tokyo and looks moderately attractive when lit-up at night.

voyage.name: Kanda Shrine
voyage.address: A block north across the river from Ochanomizu station
voyage.content: This shrine has a history dating back to the 8th century and had been highly regarded under the Edo shogunate. The current red-pillared structure has been rebuilt after being completely destroyed in the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake. The Kanda Matsuri festival, which takes place in mid-May every other year is one of the largest in Tokyo and is a sight to behold. Arrive before noon or the shrine gets packed with spectat

voyage.name: Hie Shrine
voyage.content: Another prominent shrine in Tokyo. Located atop a little hill at the edge of the area. Reached by a steep flight of stairs under a veritable tunnel of orange torii, the shrine grounds are an oasis of tranquility in the middle of Tokyo and, in good weather, a popular place for a lunchtime picnic. The Sanno Matsuri (山王祭) festival it hosts in June is counted among the 3 Great festival of Tokyo, featuring the usual panop

voyage.name: Yasukuni Shrine
voyage.content: A controversial shrine to Japan's war dead, housing the souls of some 2.5 million people killed in Japan's wars — including convicted war criminals executed by the Allies. A favorite haunt of right-wing groups in black loudspeaker-equipped trucks, and often visited by Japanese and Taiwanese politicians, drawing sharp criticisms from neighbors China and South Korea in the process. Consider keeping your visit to

voyage.name: Tokyo National Museum of Modern Art
voyage.alt: 東京国立近代美術館, Tōkyō Kokuritsu Kindai Bijutsukan
voyage.price: ¥420 for adults, ¥130 for students and children under 15 free. Admission is also free on May 18, November 3 and the first Sunday of every month. Special exhibits extra
voyage.content: With a modest permanent collection on display and regularly changing exhibitions, MOMAT is a nice place to kill a couple of hours after you've seen the Imperial Palace across the road. Entry to the nearby Crafts Gallery is included in the price.

voyage.name: Idemitsu Museum of Arts
voyage.address: On the 9th floor of the Imperial Theatre building
voyage.content: Has a noteworthy collection centering on Japanese traditional arts.

voyage.name: National Theatre of Japan
voyage.content: For those interested in theatre arts, the Kokuritsu Gekijyo holds performances in traditional arts ranging from Kabuki, Noh drama, Bunraku puppet theatre, etc. You may want to check the schedule and make a reservation beforehand.

voyage.name: Bic Camera
voyage.content: A huge, six-floor electronics store in front of JR Yurakucho Station, selling everything from household appliances to contact lenses. There is even a small movie theater on the 7th and 8th floors showing lesser-known Japanese and foreign films. Perhaps a good place for a one-stop shop if you are not able to spend time exploring the streets of Akihabara.

voyage.name: Maruzen bookshop
voyage.content: It may be your best bet to look for English books in Tokyo, including a "Books on Japan" section. If you don't find what you are looking for here, you probably won't have much luck looking elsewhere.

voyage.name: KITTE
voyage.content: The former Japan Post headquarters have been renovated into a trendy building with many shops and restaurants. The top roof is an open garden giving an amazing view on Tokyo Station, perfect for watching bullet trains come and go.

voyage.name: Peter
voyage.content: Restaurant with amazing views of Imperial Palace and excellent service. Lunch seems the best value. Kobe beef from ¥23,500. Dress code: casual.

voyage.name: Yamaya
voyage.content: For lunch you should get a bowl of rice with mentaiko (semi-spicy red fish eggs). Their specialty for dinner is motsunabe (tripe hotpot).

voyage.name: Kanda Yabu soba
voyage.content: Yabu Soba opened its doors for business in 1880.

voyage.name: RyuGin
voyage.content: Moved from Roppongi in 2018. Combining a deep respect for the Japanese culinary heritage with a will to pushing boundaries has made Nihonryori RyuGin to regarded as one of the world's best restaurants. Serves a daily-changing fix menu based on what's available at the market.

voyage.name: Tokyo Central Youth Hostel
voyage.content: Located on the 18th and 19th floors of a high-rise, with great views over the city (including a hot tub and baths overlooking the lights and skyscrapers of Shinjuku) and comfortable rooms. Formerly known as Tokyo International Hostel.

voyage.name: Imperial Hotel Tokyo
voyage.content: Never mind upstarts like the Park Hyatt, this is the grand old dame of Tokyo's hotels with over 115 years of history behind it and legendary service fit for an Emperor. Standard rooms are musty, but the refurbished Imperial Floor rooms are nice. The hotel overlooks Hibiya Park and is only a short walk from the Imperial Palace and the Ginza.

voyage.name: The New Otani
voyage.content: The flagship of the international New Otani chain, and one of the largest hotels in Tokyo, with a variety of shops and restaurants under its roof. While the main building is a 1960s concrete monolith, the extensive gardens were once part of a prince's residence and date back to the 1600s. Convenient for business travellers, as it is located within an easy walk of Akasaka, Nagatacho, and other international business d

voyage.name: Ascott Marunouchi Tokyo
voyage.content: A range of apartments with access to the swimming pool, rooftop terrace, gym, reading lounge, business centre and meeting rooms.

voyage.name: Tokyo Station Hotel
voyage.price: From ¥89,000. 10% discount with an active Japan Rail Pass or JR East Rail Pass
voyage.content: If you ever wanted to sleep in a train station, then this might be the place to do it. A part of Hyatt's Small Luxury Hotel collection, the Tokyo Station Hotel makes up a part of the 1914 red-brick building that is the terminal station of all but one of the country's Shinkansen lines. It is within easy walking distance of the Imperial Palace, and you can simply walk out of the lobby and make a U-turn to catch a train

voyage.name: Tsukiji Outer Market
voyage.alt: 築地場外市場 Tsukiji jōgai shijō
voyage.hours: Varies by shop, but typically Mon-Sat 09:00-14:00, closed holidays and most Wednesdays
voyage.content: For more than 80 years, Tsukiji was the world's largest wholesale fish market. Although the wholesale operations (including the famous tuna auctions) closed in 2018 and moved to Toyosu, the outer market remains in place and continues to welcome the public with stalls selling fresh fish, sushi, produce and kitchen supplies. Suggested plans for the former inner market site include a sport stadium or an anime/manga them

voyage.name: Tsukiji Hongwanji
voyage.content: A Jōdo Shinshū temple just a few blocks away from the fish market, worth seeing because of its unique, South Asian-inspired architecture. Buddhist services are held in English on Saturday evenings.

voyage.name: Nihonbashi Bridge
voyage.content: Nihonbashi means Japan bridge. It is the most famous bridge in Japan and one of the very few historic bridges remaining in Tokyo. The current stone and steel bridge was built in 1911. It is the point from which all distances are measured to the capital. Since 1964 it is unfortunately overshadowed by a massive expressway, blocking much of the view.

voyage.name: Tokyo Stock Exchange
voyage.alt: 東京証券取引所 Tokyo shoken torihikijo
voyage.content: Tokyo's stock exchange, while one of the largest in the world by capitalization, is now entirely automated, and the tiny building it resides in is mostly for show, featuring a small museum, exhibition hall, and broadcasting facilities. English tours can be booked in advance.

voyage.name: Hama-rikyū Gardens
voyage.price: Park admission ¥300 (age 65+ ¥150, primary school children free)
voyage.content: It was built by 17th-century shoguns for their private enjoyment. Hama-rikyu is now a public walking garden with an all-season range of flowers and flowering trees. The highlight is the tea house, picturesquely set on a small island in the middle of a pond, where green tea and sweets are available starting at ¥500, and ¥1000 for a set. The garden is next to Tsukiji fish market. A boat which runs up the Sumida River t

voyage.name: Mitsui Memorial Museum
voyage.alt: 三井記念美術館, Mitsui Kinen Bijutsukan
voyage.content: Art museum, the collection includes items used in the Japanese tea ceremony as well as Eastern antiques. Housed in an historic building dating back to 1926.

voyage.name: Tsukiji Outer Market
voyage.content: The Outer Market of the Tsukiji Fish Market contain a bewildering array of shops. One shop carries nothing but dried seaweed, another knives, another is just bowls of all shapes and sizes! After you've had your sushi breakfast, wander around these shops and pick up something interesting.

voyage.name: Ramen Cooking Tokyo
voyage.content: English-only small-group cooking class (maximum 8 participants) where visitors prepare ramen and sushi in a 3-hour session, with a sake pairing of three varieties. Located in Tsukishima, a short walk from the monja-yaki district.

voyage.name: Sho-Chu Authority
voyage.content: This humbly named shop stocks over 3,000 varieties of the Japanese tipples shochu and awamori.

voyage.name: Oshio Honten
voyage.content: The original shop of one of the better-known chains here, with half a dozen restaurants. Try the mentaiko-shiso monja with cod roe and perilla, which tastes oh so much better than it looks.

voyage.name: Sushisay Main Store
voyage.content: Over 120 years old, this is now a large chain, but the head shop is in Tsukiji and it is well-reputed.

voyage.name: Sushizanmai
voyage.content: The self-proclaimed "King Of Tuna", this is now a large chain but they originate from here in Tsukiji, where they have at least 7 locations and this three-story Honten. Prices are per roll and range from ¥100-500, or order a set meal for ¥3000. They have an excellent English menu.

voyage.name: Tamahide
voyage.content: In business since 1760, perhaps the oldest in Tokyo. This restaurant specialises in Oyakodon, literally "parent-child bowl", made from spiced chicken with scrambled eggs (hence the name) and sweet sauce on rice. A popular comfort food with surprising complexity. Expect long queues.

voyage.name: Tsujihan
voyage.alt: 日本橋海鮮丼 つじ半 日本橋本店
voyage.content: It is a Kaisen-dong store located near Tokyo Station. It is characterized by pouring stock with a little rice left.

voyage.name: Sumisho Hotel
voyage.content: A ryokan-style hotel, Japanese style rooms and big traditional bath available.

voyage.name: Tokyu Stay Nihombashi
voyage.content: Slight discounts are offered for extended stays. Part of the Tokyu Stay chain, these hotels are popular with business travelers. The small kitchenettes, washer/dryers, and free LAN access in all rooms makes these a good value.

voyage.name: Tokyu Stay Tsukiji
voyage.price: Singles from ¥9400, twins from ¥14,700 per night, breakfast included. Discounts for extended stays.
voyage.content: Part of the Tokyu Stay chain. Free internet access, microwave, washer-dryer, and kitchenette in each room. Good staff, views of nearby temple. Located very close to Tsukiji fish market, avoiding an early morning taxi ride.

voyage.name: Somerset Ginza East Tokyo
voyage.content: This property contains 124 studio and one-bedroom apartments. Offers weekly housekeeping services.

voyage.name: Royal Park Hotel
voyage.alt: ロイヤルパークホテル
voyage.content: Five-star luxury hotel

voyage.name: Tokyo Tower
voyage.content: This was a newly re-industrialized Japan's 1958 answer to Paris's Eiffel Tower — a bit more modern-looking and 9 m taller. Entry to the Main Observatory (150m) is ¥820, while ascending to the Special Observatory (250m) is an extra ¥600. Your photo will be taken for purchase later (¥600). Tip: To get a good view of, and picture with, the tower, try the courtyard in front of Zojoji (nearby), or the se

voyage.name: Zōjō-ji Temple
voyage.content: This grand old temple is the headquarters of the Jōdo-shū sect and houses the graves of 6 of the Tokugawa shoguns, but is a little off the beaten track and is rarely visited by tourists. Particularly beautiful around cherry blossom time. It hosts a variety of religious and non-religious festivals throughout the year.

voyage.name: Sengaku-ji
voyage.content: A temple most famous as the resting place of the 47 Rōnin, a famous group of samurai who banded together to avenge their unfairly slain master. Having obtained the head of the offender, they brought it to this very temple and then were condemned to commit ritual suicide, like their master. The story is told in Chūshingura, the best-known of all Kabuki plays. History aside, the temple isn't much to look at, but the sm

voyage.name: Institute for Nature Study
voyage.price: Adults ¥300, senior citizens and children free
voyage.hours: Sep 1-Apr 30: 09:00-16:30, May 1-Aug 31: 09:00-17:00; closed Mondays, closed Dec 28-Jan 4
voyage.content: A 200,000 sq m nature preserve in the heart of the city, with birds and waterfowl, insects and marine life.

voyage.name: Rainbow Bridge
voyage.content: Completed in 1993, this gateway to Odaiba is among the most beautiful modern bridges in Japan. Decorated with 444 lights, which change according to the seasons. Can be crossed by bus or metro.

voyage.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Teien Art Museum
voyage.content: Art museum housed in a classic Art Deco style structure, connected to a small park with Japanese and Western gardens and outdoor sculptures.

voyage.name: Nezu Museum
voyage.content: Showcases the private art collection of Nezu Kaichirō with many pieces from the Edo period.

voyage.name: Taro Okamoto Memorial Museum
voyage.content: Former studio and house of Okamoto Taro. Unfinished works and paintings are shown. He made numerous masterpieces such as "Tower of the Sun" at the Expo 1970 and "Myth of the Future" mural now exhibited in Shibuya.

voyage.name: TEPIA
voyage.content: Science museum showcasing new technologies, robots, home automation. Explanations are in Japanese but playing with the objects is still fun for kids and adults.

voyage.name: Aquapark shinagawa
voyage.content: A popular aquarium with exhibits that combine dolphin shows and technology. The tunnel tank includes manta rays, green sawfish, and the only dwarf sawfish on display in the world.

voyage.name: Japan Traditional Crafts Aoyama Square
voyage.alt: 伝統工芸 青山スクエア
voyage.content: Gallery and shop for handicraft products from all over Japan.

voyage.name: Mori Building Digital Art Museum: teamLab Borderless
voyage.alt: 森ビル デジタルアート ミュージアム：エプソン チームラボボーダレス (チームラボボーダレス, 麻布台ヒルズ, 東京)
voyage.price: ¥3600-5600, depending on how far in advance you buy
voyage.address: Azabudai Hills Garden Plaza B B1 5-9, Toranomon, Minato-ku,
voyage.content: Art museum with immersive art exhibits.

voyage.name: Tokyo Cruise
voyage.alt: 水上バス 東京湾クルーズ (waterborne bus Tokyo Bay cruise)
voyage.content: Plies the Sumida River and Tokyo Bay between Hamamatsucho, Odaiba, Asakusa and other points.

voyage.name: Tokyo Island
voyage.alt: 東京愛らんど Tōkyō Airando
voyage.content: Antenna shop of Izu Islands and Ogasawara Islands.

voyage.name: Azabu-Jūban
voyage.content: A quieter commercial district to the southeast of Roppongi Hills, and a good place to spend a lazier afternoon browsing through shops and enjoying the local cafés. The surrounding residential area is popular among professional expats, so expect to see many international families as you walk through.

voyage.name: Japan Sake and Shōchū Information Center
voyage.alt: 日本の酒情報館 nihon no sake jōhōkan
voyage.content: This four-story complex run by the Central Brewers' Union sells anything and everything related to sake, including cups, glasses, books, hydrometers and, of course, the nectar itself. \315/515 gets you a taste of 3/5 sakes that change daily.

voyage.name: Daiei
voyage.price: One of the cheapest supermarket in the whole area
voyage.content: Two floors of food, drinks and more.

voyage.name: Kua'aina
voyage.price: Meal sets are available for ¥1000, higher after 17:00
voyage.content: Hawaiian hamburgers, order-at-the counter from a picture menu with English.

voyage.name: Worldstar Cafe
voyage.content: Popular with business people or singles during lunchtime. Meal sets are ¥980–1200, comes w/ main, salad, drink; main being spaghetti, etc. Useful for a late night spot to hang around, since they're open until 06:00.

voyage.name: Gonpachi
voyage.content: This lively and popular izakaya, with a spectacular spacious interior and high-profile location, has served luminaries such as George W. Bush and former Prime Minister Koizumi, and was the model for the battle scene in Quentin Tarantino's film Kill Bill. (The owner turned down the director's request to use the place itself.) Apart from this, it is a chain, so prices are reasonable food is not special, with all-you-ca

voyage.name: Sarashina
voyage.alt: 麻布永坂 更科本店
voyage.content: One of the most famous restaurants for soba (buckwheat noodle). Try the various noodles they have, for instance egg noodles, with different colors. Their factory is still across the road despite sky-rocketing real estate prices.

voyage.name: Tony Roma's
voyage.content: Step out of Japan and into the United States; the bilingual staff and English-only menu might make you forget you are in Tokyo. The restaurant features their trademark ribs, worth the price which starts at ¥1880. The Texas Mud Pie is the cure for tiny Japanese desserts.

voyage.name: Kushinobō
voyage.content: for kushiage (deep-fried skewers).

voyage.name: Nodaiwa
voyage.content: Perhaps the best spot in Japan to be served unagi, or freshwater eel. Famous for always using naturally grown eels, never farmed ones. In the business for more than 200 years, Nodaiwa remains as popular as ever.

voyage.name: Anniversaire Cafe
voyage.alt: アニヴェルセルカフェ
voyage.content: This is a fashionable cafe of Paris style. You can enjoy elegant mood with seeing a row of houses and street of Omotesando. You can also choose fish or meat for lunch. Has another branch at Minato Mirai in Yokohama.

voyage.name: Daigo
voyage.address: Atago 2 chome 3-1, Atago Green Hills Forest Tower, 2F, Atago
voyage.content: Exquisite vegetarian or vegan "shojin ryori" cuisine. This is the traditional Buddhist spin on kaiseki. Gracefully served by attentive kimono-clad staff. Small private dining rooms look out onto Japanese gardens. Very expensive, but a top-class experience.

voyage.name: Narisawa
voyage.content: Ranked among the world's best restaurants and with two Michelin stars. Expect a blend of classical French techniques with the finest Japanese ingredients. Narisawa also has a commitment to sustainability, which expresses itself at the table.

voyage.name: Ristorante da Nino
voyage.price: Weekday lunch courses from ¥1400 (Saturday lunch courses from ¥2800); dinner courses from ¥8000
voyage.content: Within easy walking distance from both Tokyo Midtown and Roppongi crossing, owner chef Antonino Lentini offers fine and fresh Sicilian dishes. Good wine selection.

voyage.name: Hotel Okura
voyage.content: Luxury hotel that has been host to many celebrities since its opening in 1962.

voyage.name: Sheraton Miyako Hotel Tokyo
voyage.alt: シェラトン都ホテル東京
voyage.content: Reasonably swish hotel. Good for a layover with its back garden and downstairs cigar bar. Probably a poor option for a tourist unless you have business in the area as it's about a ten minute walk from nearby transport and not close to attractions.

voyage.name: Tokyo Prince Hotel
voyage.content: The hotel staff speak English, and the hotel has the amenities of its modern competitors. But it is a bit of a throwback. The beds are short, the decor is tacky, and everything (except the DSL) feels a little dated.

voyage.name: Akasaka Yoko Hotel
voyage.content: It's quiet and it's a hotel near the station

voyage.name: Tokyo Regional Immigration Bureau
voyage.alt: 東京出入国在留管理局
voyage.content: This center serves foreign residents and long-term visitors. Also houses immigration detention. If going in the morning, get there early because a line forms outside long before opening hours.

voyage.name: Hara Museum of Contemporary Art
voyage.content: This small museum hosts a variety of interesting exhibitions in a 1930s house which is a great example of modern architecture in pre-war Japan. There is a very nice indoor/outdoor cafe. (2026: closed/moved to Gunma prefecture, see Wikipedia)

voyage.name: Shinagawa Aquarium
voyage.alt: しながわ水族館, Shinagawa Suizokukan

voyage.name: Showa Neon Takamura Kanban Museum
voyage.alt: 昭和ネオン高村看板ミュージアム
voyage.content: The sign company Showa Neon has a museum with shop signs from the Edo and early Meiji periods. Reportedly all descriptions in this museum are in Japanese. Closed in June 2023 for renovation; reopen due in March 2025.

voyage.name: Aqua Park Shinagawa
voyage.price: Adults ¥1,800; Elementary and middle school students ¥1,000; Kids over 4 years old ¥600
voyage.content: Aquarium with dolphin and seal shows and hundreds of species of fish. There is also a carousel ride.

voyage.name: Takanawa Catholic Church
voyage.content: This modern church rebuilt on a historic site is handicapped-accessible and has Sunday Mass in English on the fourth Sunday of each month at 13:00.

voyage.name: Ōi Horse Race Course
voyage.alt: 大井競馬場, Tokyo City Keiba
voyage.content: The best racecourse affiliated to National Association of Racing, the umbrella organization for local horseracing operators. Tokyo Dai-Shoten race in December is rated as international Grade I. Many restaurants and food stands. Night races from March to December are decorated with beautiful illuminations.

voyage.name: Coffee Roast Sai
voyage.content: Roasts beans while you wait (30-60 min), usually with a wonderful free cup of coffee. For true connoisseurs.

voyage.name: Sanrio Gift gate
voyage.alt: サンリオ ギフトゲート
voyage.content: A shop of the brand behind the famous Hello Kitty.

voyage.name: eCute Shinagawa
voyage.hours: 08:00-22:00 for most shops, some open earlier
voyage.content: A small food court and take out restaurants featuring a couple of dozen food stands and bakery or sweet shops on the first level. This is also a very comfortably air-conditioned place to wait for a train connection. There are some full-service restaurants on the upper level. A few examples of shops include:.

voyage.name: Andersen
voyage.content: If you are making an early departure for Kamakura or points south pick up sandwiches to go

voyage.name: Kongariya
voyage.content: Select from a wide range of onigiri with interesting fillings like squid and kimchee, miso or shoyu grilled riceballs, or even ones wrapped in Indian naan and baked.

voyage.name: Paul
voyage.content: Sandwiches on real baguettes.

voyage.name: Yoshinoya
voyage.content: Fast food chain with Japanese style food.

voyage.name: Atre Shinagawa
voyage.content: A collection of restaurants grouped around a Queens Isetan grocery. Dean & Deluca, on the second floor, has a take-out sandwich and coffee bar which is convenient for supplies to get you through a long Shinkansen ride. The fourth floor has the Lounge Foodium restaurant complex including Grand Central Oyster Bar.

voyage.name: Devi Corner
voyage.content: Excellent Indian cuisine.

voyage.name: Royal Host
voyage.content: Popular "family restaurant" chain with surprisingly good coffee but little else that stands out.

voyage.name: Tsubame Grill (Shinagawa-ekimae)
voyage.alt: つばめグリル 品川駅前店
voyage.content: Tsubame Grill chain is famous for its "hamburg" dish. Contrary to belief, lunch special only costs ¥1150 — a bargain for the excellent quality of food. The "hamburg" dish comes piping hot covered completely in an aluminum foil.

voyage.name: Tikka & Biryani
voyage.content: Has excellent Indian Mughal Biryani.

voyage.name: 82 Ale House
voyage.hours: Last orders are at 22:45 on Saturdays and Sundays
voyage.content: Very convincing Victorian style British pub run by the same company as another popular pub chain, HUB. Largish drinks menu which includes single malt whiskeys, real ale and Guinness on tap for ¥900 a pint.

voyage.name: Guesthouse Shinagawa-shuku
voyage.content: Small, friendly guesthouse "for backpackers" in a very 'local' feeling location.

voyage.name: Toyoko Inn Shinagawa Aomono-yokocho-eki
voyage.content: An alternative Toyoko Inn, five minutes south of Shinagawa by Keikyu local train. Availability is generally better here than the other Toyoko Inn, and the hotel is directly connected to the Keikyu line.

voyage.name: Toyoko Inn Shinagawa-eki Takanawa-guchi
voyage.content: A bit cheaper than the rest, and it can sell out quickly.

voyage.name: Keikyu EX Inn Shinagawa-Ekimae
voyage.content: Formerly known as the Meridien Pacific, but since renovated and converted to a Keikyu EX Inn.

voyage.name: Grand Prince Hotel Takanawa
voyage.content: Though priced similarly per-night to other hotels in the area, rooms are available at an incredible discount if staying more than 3 nights through the week.

voyage.name: Keikyu EX Hotel Takanawa
voyage.content: A more economical alternative to the more expensive high-service hotels, while still being good for business travelers who need the room primarily for sleeping and internet.

voyage.name: Hotel La Foret
voyage.address: 品川区北品川4-7-36 Kita Shinagawa 4-7-36
voyage.content: This high end hotel is in the deluxe Gotenyama Hills complex.

voyage.name: The Strings Hotel
voyage.content: A top-notch hotel near Shinagawa Station which is worth visiting for a drink or a meal to get the view of the bay and Rainbow Bridge. Part of the Intercontinental chain.

voyage.name: Zōshigaya Cemetery
voyage.content: The final resting place of Lafcadio Hearn is about the most exciting attraction in this neck of the woods.

voyage.name: Kōgan-ji Temple
voyage.content: This small temple in Sugamo is known for two statues: Togenuki Jizō, who heals sick children, and the boddhisattva Kannon, who will cure your pains if you wash themagical appropriate part of the statue. More morbidly, you can also pray to Kannon for a swift and painless death, so you will not be a burden to your relatives in your old age. Visitors pray Enmei Jizōson for their health too. The way to pray is unusual. P

voyage.name: Myōkō-ji Temple
voyage.content: According to legend, the grave of Lady Oiwa (Oiwa-san) in Yotsuya Kaidan, Japan's best-known ghost story and a direct inspiration for the Ring horror movies, is in this temple. In a nutshell, the beautiful Oiwa was disfigured, divorced and killed, and then comes back to haunt the people who wronged her.

voyage.name: Honmyōji Temple
voyage.content: This temple is known for a fire called Meireki-no-Taika, an inferno 400 years ago which killed over 100,000 people. It is said that this fire broke out in Honmyōji. There are also some tombs of famous people in this temple. A Japanese swordman Chiba Shūsaku and a political office leader Tōyama Kinshirō, for example.

voyage.name: Hōmyōji
voyage.content: Famous Japanese temple built in 810. Features the statue of Kishimojin (鬼子母神像) who is a Japanese God of fertility. Visitors go to Hōmyōji to pray for their children's birth, growth and security. The Kishimojin figure typically take the form of the devil, but this statue holds a baby, and the figure is beautiful. In this temple the Oeshiki-Taisai festival (御会式大祭) is held from October 16 to October 18 every year.

voyage.name: Sunshine 60
voyage.content: Sunshine 60 was once the tallest building in Japan and it remains the most prominent building within the Sunshine City complex. The surrounding Sunshine City complex includes shops, restaurants, an aquarium, and an observatory at the top of the Sunshine 60 building.

voyage.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Theatre
voyage.address: on the west side of the Ikebukuro train/subway station
voyage.content: Offers various exhibits and concerts behind the impressive glass facade.

voyage.name: Tokyo Shaheed Minar
voyage.content: A beautiful monument, symbolizing love to the mother language. It is based on the mother language movement, that originated in Dhaka, Bangladesh in 1952, followed by the UNESCO declaration of International Mother Language Day (21 February). It was a present from Bangladesh to the Japanese people, in 2005, recognizing Tokyo Boishakhi Mela (Bangladesh New Year Festival), organized every year in mid April, by Japan Bang

voyage.name: Ikefukurō
voyage.content: A statue of an owl (fukurō) near the east exit. Many people use this as a meeting spot.

voyage.name: Namja Town
voyage.alt: ナンジャタウンホーム
voyage.content: The Namja Town has many attractions. For example there are some Japanese style haunted houses, interactive 1964 shooting games, egg-raising game (the whole process is quite similar to raising a child, where you will need to take the egg to toilets, restaurants, and hospitals, until after a certain point. Then you can take the eggs to play games. This is quite a 'couply' game to do). And there are big food shops: the

voyage.name: Manten
voyage.content: There is a planetarium called Manten (meaning "full sky") in Sunshine City. This planetarium shows three types of programs and repeats them in a day. These three types of programs are called The Planetarium Program, The CG Planetarium Program, The Healing Program. The Planetarium Program shows some themes of programs with Japanese famous musicians. The CG Planetarium Program shows science programs. The Healing Progra

voyage.name: Animate
voyage.content: Lots of new anime/manga-related merchandise.

voyage.name: K-Books
voyage.content: Good selection of anime, manga, and posters.

voyage.name: Mandarake
voyage.content: One of the Mandarake chain of used anime/manga goods stores, the Ikebukuro branch specializes in doujinshi, in particular doujinshi for girls.

voyage.name: Bic Camera
voyage.content: This discount retailer's flagship store on the east side of the station, with several branches nearby.

voyage.name: Junkudō
voyage.content: A 9-story bookstore (top floor has English titles).

voyage.name: Sugamo
voyage.content: Popularly known as "Grandma's Harajuku" (obaachan no Harajuku), and indeed most shops in the area do seem targeted towards an older clientèle. For the (rare) tourist, however, this means a plentiful supply of tea, pottery, kitchen implements and clothes in styles that went out of fashion 50 years ago. The area is at its liveliest on the 4th, 14th and 24th of each month when a street market is held.

voyage.name: Maruji
voyage.address: Sugamo 4-21-11 and three other outlets nearby
voyage.content: Probably the most famous and successful shop in Sugamo, Maruji specializes in one thing: red underwear (赤パンツ aka-pantsu). By energizing a pressure point below your navel, Maruji's crimson panties, boxers and long-johns will keep you warm and fill you with vigor — or so they say.

voyage.name: Konaya
voyage.content: The original shop of restaurant chain renowned for its curry udon noodles. The noodles are cut by hand, the special curry stock is brewed for two days, and ¥1210 will get you some mighty fine tasting udon.

voyage.name: Fight Gyoza
voyage.content: Famous for deep-fried gyoza. So many people stand in a line in front of the restaurant.

voyage.name: Souten
voyage.content: High-end yakitori. Five stick set from around ¥1,600. Do try the chicken sashimi--outside the comfort zone for many visitors, but you may be pleasantly surprised. Extensive selection of nihonshu featuring Kozaemon. Its website has some English info.

voyage.name: Tobu and Seibu basements
voyage.content: Urban Japanese keep their grocery stores beneath their department stores. If you go to the B1 and B2 levels of the massive stores flanking the Ikebukuro station, you will find endless acres of raw and prepared food. Buy a bunch and take it back to your hotel fridge.

voyage.name: Shakey's Pizza
voyage.content: Down Sunshine-Dori on the way to Sunshine 60, on the left, there's a Shakey's Pizza. There are lunchtime buffets with great pizza the way only Japanese like to serve it.

voyage.name: Ghiottone
voyage.content: Excellent pasta and salads, in portions that are ample for two. The crab spaghetti is very popular. No non-smoking tables.

voyage.name: Malay-Chan
voyage.content: A small Malaysian restaurant on the west side of the train/subway station that is a little hard to find. Halal food.

voyage.name: Mutekiya
voyage.content: Good ramen.

voyage.name: Al-Flah
voyage.content: A halal supermarket and restaurant that sells halal food, including vegetarian curries. The store also conveniently has a bollywood-movie section.

voyage.name: Namja Town
voyage.content: Namja Town has some big food shops in Sunshin City– the gyoza studium, the ice cream city, and the dessert empire of Tokyo. Gyoza is a kind of Japanese food. The gyoza stadium collects gyozas of many famous gyoza restaurants in Japan. The ice cream city collects many kinds of ice creams in the world. The dessert empire of Tokyo collects some famous cakes. And it has events regularly. For example many kinds of pudding

voyage.name: Sakura Cafe Ikebukuro
voyage.content: Opened in 2008, one of Tokyo's largest open-air-terrace cafes with easy-going and relaxed style located at 1st floor of "Sakura Hotel Ikebukuro" which welcomes guests from over 110 countries every year. International atmosphere with 60 beers from around the world from ¥550, monthly changing snacks and meals from ¥300 also from a wide variety of countries, and coffee for ¥180.

voyage.name: Sakura Hotel Ikebukuro
voyage.content: Various rooms are good for groups and private. All staff speak English.

voyage.name: Kimi Ryokan
voyage.content: This friendly if very tourist-oriented minshuku (no, it's not a ryokan) is an excellent option for first time travelers to Tokyo. It is reasonably priced (¥4500) and has English speaking staff. A nice way to spend your first night on a tatami.

voyage.name: Hotel Metropolitan Tokyo Ikebukuro
voyage.alt: ホテルメトロポリタン東京池袋
voyage.content: A short walk away from Ikebukuro station, a decent 4-star hotel with nice, clean rooms and friendly staff who mostly speak fluent English. Limousine bus services are available to both Narita and Haneda airports.

voyage.name: Dai-ichi Inn Ikebukuro
voyage.content: A 1-minute walk from the station (take East Exit), right across from the back of Parco. In-room broadband internet, massage service, 24-hour convenience store, and many other amenities. TV channel list includes CNN. Some of the staff speak near-fluent English, others not so much.

voyage.name: Hotel Grand City
voyage.content: The staff don't speak English very well.

voyage.name: APA Hotel Tokyo Itabashi-ekimae
voyage.alt: アパホテル東京板橋駅前
voyage.content: This three-star hotel is near the Itabshi Station, 3 min to Ikebukuro and 8 min to Shinjuku.

voyage.name: Kumano Shrine
voyage.content: Built 800 years ago. Surrounded by trees, people visit to pray or just for the peace and quiet. Some come for specific the worship practice of Yakuyoke, a purification ritual to drive out evil spirits. Like all shrines, they sell protective amulets for health, good studies, or traffic safety, but these are distinctively cute. For a traditional shrine, they have a particularly flashy website that gives a good preview.

voyage.name: Meguro Parasitological Museum
voyage.content: One of a kind and oddly popular with couples on dates, although you might want to skip lunch before (or after) your visit here as the exhibits and pictures can be rather graphic. A compact two-story building, the most famous exhibit inside is an 8.8-meter-long tapeworm, with a matching string for you to take the measurement.

voyage.name: Meguro Gajoen
voyage.content: A luxury hotel and wedding hall, with restaurants, cafes, and banquet rooms. One of the most popular attractions, though, is the spectacular public restroom.

voyage.name: Gohyakurakanji
voyage.content: This temple contains over 300 statues, all with different facial expressions. They were all carved by the same monk from 1687 to 1695.

voyage.name: Japan Folk Crafts Museum
voyage.content: Founded in 1936. Must see for Japanese handicraft lovers.

voyage.name: Kameyamannendo
voyage.content: This Japanese-style confectionery shop was established in 1938.

voyage.name: Wara
voyage.content: There are many kinds of kimono which is gathered all over Japan. Money pouch (巾着) and bag which are made by cloth of kimono are popular. In this shop, you can learn how to put on kimono.

voyage.name: Sweets Forest
voyage.content: This is a mall dedicated to desserts. Multiple shops and cafes.

voyage.name: Nana's Green Tea
voyage.content: This cafe has a lot of sweets and drinks made with powdered green tea and adzuki bean. Taste four kinds of Japanese tea. Try the Maccha chocolate latte.

voyage.name: Hara-Donut
voyage.alt: はらドーナッツ 目黒店
voyage.content: Organic donut shop. Seemingly oxymoronic healthy donuts are made with soy milk.

voyage.name: Tonki
voyage.hours: Closed Tue and third Mon of the month
voyage.content: Possibly good place to go for tonkatsu (breaded deep-fried pork cutlets), and popular with foreigners.

voyage.name: Junkadelic
voyage.content: Though the building looks a little old, this Mexican restaurant has some great Tex-Mex cuisine. The menu is not very large, but what it has is worth eating. Portions are reasonably sized, so consider getting an appetizer along with the main dish. For drinks, there are several Mexican beers and Mexican tequila available.

voyage.name: Potager
voyage.alt: パティスリー ポタジエ
voyage.content: A bakery offering vegetable cakes

voyage.name: Shutters
voyage.content: Try the apple pie a la mode. Popular dishes here are the odd combination of spare ribs and apple pie. You can eat many flavors of tender spare ribs such as soy sauce, basil, and mustard. You can choose from sauces on your apple pie: cinnamon, blueberry, raspberry, chocolate and caramel--with vanilla ice cream too.

voyage.name: Sushikou
voyage.content: Sushi.

voyage.name: Jiyugaoka Burger
voyage.content: Domestically-sourced, organic and thick burgers in a lush balcony setting.

voyage.name: Kochoo
voyage.content: Specializes in sundubu, a Korean stew which actually has roots in Los Angeles. All-you-can-eat banchan, which is common practice in Korea but rare in Japan!

voyage.name: Mangetsu Korean Cuisine
voyage.content: Korean-run establishment with an intimate atmosphere, great for an evening date. Good chijimi!

voyage.name: Clann
voyage.content: Irish pub with live music many nights.

voyage.name: British Restaurant CLASH
voyage.content: Formerly known as The Meguro Tavern. A British-style pub with plenty of draft beers and football on the telly.

voyage.name: Rakuya
voyage.content: Spacious, classy but casual restaurant-bar with live music every night.

voyage.name: Speyside Way
voyage.content: Hundreds of whiskeys fill every available space. Hundreds. Short selection of micro-beers is also available.

voyage.name: Westin Hotel Tokyo
voyage.alt: ウェスティンホテル東京
voyage.content: Renovated in 2023. Rooms are elegant and well furnished with over-sized bathrooms and workout areas. Their in house spa offers a variety of services.

voyage.name: Tokyu Stay Meguro-Yutenji
voyage.price: Singles start at ¥9,450, doubles at ¥17,850. Slight discounts are offered for extended stays
voyage.content: Part of the Tokyu Stay chain, these hotels are popular with business travelers. The small kitchenettes, washer/dryers, and free LAN access in all rooms makes these a good value.

voyage.name: Hotel Princess Garden
voyage.alt: ホテルプリンセスガーデン
voyage.content: Princess Garden offers rooms that are very comfortable. The beautiful garden and Japanese Tea Room on the hotel grounds add a level of beauty and serenity.

voyage.name: Hotel Pulitzer Jiyugaoka
voyage.alt: ホテル ピュリッツァー 自由が丘
voyage.content: Small hotel with only 18 rooms in the center of Jiyugaoka.
